main.title: The Darkness II
main.subtitle: Jackie Estacado confronts the Brotherhood
main.summary: The Darkness II is a 2012 first-person shooter video game developed by Digital Extremes and published by 2K.

cards.heading: Jackie Estacado confronts the Brotherhood
cards.text: The Darkness II is a 2012 first-person shooter video game developed by Digital Extremes and published by 2K. The game is the sequel to The Darkness (2007) and based on the comic book series published by Top Cow Productions. The player controls Jackie Estacado, a mafia hitman who possesses a mysterious power called "the Darkness" that grants him supernatural abilities and a pair of Demon Arms. The game features elements found in role-playing video games such as skill trees, experience, and a four-player cooperative mode. The player must rescue the soul of Jackie's dead girlfriend, which was trapped by the Darkness in Hell, and confront the Brotherhood, a group of armed cultists trying to take the Darkness away from Jackie.

cards.heading: Demon Arms change the rules of combat
cards.text: Jackie's Demon Arms work alongside his firearms. They can slash enemies, tear away a car door for a shield or throw objects across a room. Devouring a fallen enemy's heart restores health, making a defeated opponent another resource during a fight. A Darkling helps gather weapons and ammunition; some sequences let the player control it through spaces Jackie cannot enter. Light interrupts this advantage, disabling his Darkness powers and health regeneration while blurring his vision. Shooting out a lamp can therefore change the immediate balance of a room before he approaches its occupants.

cards.heading: A hand-painted graphic noir
cards.text: The Darkness comic was a large inspiration for the team. The team read the comic and decided to adopt a comic book-influenced "graphic noir" art style, as they believed the comic's use of high contrast colors contributed to its success. The team used some of the assets made by Starbreeze as a reference, and created new ones using their own internal proprietary game engine named the Evolution Engine, which powered the studio's previous game Dark Sector (2008). The development artists hand-painted the majority of the game's assets, though this idea was initially met with resistance within the art team due to the huge amount of workload such an approach would create.

cards.heading: Vendettas tells a parallel story
cards.text: The game features a cooperative multiplayer campaign called "Vendettas" that runs parallel to the main campaign and allows up to four players to play together. The story involves four hitmen working for Jackie as they attempt to stop the Brotherhood from obtaining the Spear of Destiny. Each character has different Darkness powers and is armed with a unique special weapon. For instance, Inugami is a character who uses a Darkness-infused samurai sword, while Shoshanna uses a blunderbuss which can shoot without bullets. Although the mode can be played solo, the experience is significantly more difficult. There is an arcade mode called "Hit List" that allows players to replay certain Vendetta missions and complete challenges.

main.title: Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning
main.subtitle: An action RPG from Big Huge Games and 38 Studios
main.summary: Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning was released in North America on February 7, 2012, combining character building and real-time action combat.

cards.heading: An action RPG from Big Huge Games and 38 Studios
cards.text: Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning was released in North America on February 7, 2012. Developed by Big Huge Games and 38 Studios, it combines character building, equipment and statistics with real-time combat. The project brought together Ken Rolston, R.A. Salvatore and Todd McFarlane. Players develop their character while using dodges, chained attacks and weapons designed to respond with the immediacy of an action game.

cards.heading: Salvatore, McFarlane and Rolston build Amalur
cards.text: R.A. Salvatore developed the distant history of Amalur, Todd McFarlane shaped its visual direction, and Ken Rolston brought experience from Morrowind and Oblivion to the game’s structure. Electronic Arts presented the three as the creative core of the project. Their contributions cover the setting’s background, the appearance of monsters and armor, and the systems through which players explore the world and develop a character.

cards.heading: Weapons, magic and dodges shape combat
cards.text: Combat combines weapons, magic, dodges and abilities. Changing weapons changes attack range, animations and the possibilities for chaining attacks. Character statistics, equipment and progression remain part of the system. Ken Rolston had described many digital RPGs as deep but often slow and awkward during action; Reckoning was designed to make movement and attacks more immediate while retaining those role-playing systems.

cards.heading: Destinies support specializations and hybrid builds
cards.text: The Destiny system allows the protagonist’s build to change during the journey. Points and abilities are distributed across Might, Finesse and Sorcery, and their combinations unlock Destinies that reward either focused specializations or hybrid builds. Years later, THQ Nordic retained this structure in Re-Reckoning while changing balance, zone levels and loot generation. The character can be reorganized instead of remaining tied to a rigid class.

main.title: Gravity Rush
main.subtitle: Kat falls into a different kind of open world
main.summary: Gravity Rush, known in Japan as Gravity Daze, is a 2012 action-adventure video game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita.

cards.heading: Kat falls into a different kind of open world
cards.text: Gravity Rush, known in Japan as Gravity Daze, reached PlayStation Vita in 2012. Players guide Kat, an amnesiac who can change the direction in which she falls, as she helps Hekseville's inhabitants and fights the Nevi. Her powers shape travel through the open city and attacks against enemies. Bluepoint Games later developed Gravity Rush Remastered for PlayStation 4.

cards.heading: Gravity changes navigation and combat
cards.text: Kat explores Hekseville by changing the direction in which she falls. Tilting the Vita aims her towards a wall, ceiling or distant surface, turning the city into routes that ordinary walking cannot reach. An energy meter limits how long her powers remain active and must recharge when exhausted. Combat uses the same change of orientation: Kat can kick from the ground or line up an airborne attack on an enemy's weak point. Approaching from farther away increases the damage, but also demands a more carefully judged flight. Some targeting abilities have cooldowns, so positioning matters between attacks.

cards.heading: Comics help shape Hekseville
cards.text: Beginning development for PlayStation 3 in 2008 under the title Gravité before moving to the Vita, Gravity Rush was conceived by director Keiichiro Toyama prior to his work on Silent Hill and the Siren series. The team overcame technical challenges due to the gameplay and chosen hardware. The world, story and artistic style drew from Japanese and Western comics including the work of French artist Jean Giraud. The music was composed by Kohei Tanaka, who worked on the project from an early stage.

main.title: Twisted Metal
main.subtitle: The tournament returns with heavier machinery
main.summary: Twisted Metal is Eat Sleep Play's PlayStation 3 vehicular combat game, first released in North America on 14 February 2012. Cars and other armed vehicles fight through arenas where surviving an attack matters more than completing a clean lap. The release reboots the series around its familiar mixture of violent competition and grotesque personalities. Weapons, routes and the handling of each vehicle shape the next confrontation. A street becomes useful because it offers an escape, a pickup or a way to bring an opponent into range, rather than simply belonging to a racecourse.

cards.heading: The tournament returns with heavier machinery
cards.text: Twisted Metal is Eat Sleep Play's PlayStation 3 vehicular combat game, first released in North America on 14 February 2012. Cars and other armed vehicles fight through arenas where surviving an attack matters more than completing a clean lap. The release reboots the series around its familiar mixture of violent competition and grotesque personalities. Weapons, routes and the handling of each vehicle shape the next confrontation. A street becomes useful because it offers an escape, a pickup or a way to bring an opponent into range, rather than simply belonging to a racecourse.

cards.heading: An objective can turn the whole battle
cards.text: The game places considerable emphasis on multiplayer, with split-screen and online modes supporting different scales of competition. Nuke gives teams a multi-stage objective involving an enemy leader, a missile launcher and a target suspended beneath a helicopter. Completing one part does not end the contest; it creates another task that opponents can interrupt. The player must connect driving and weapon use to the current stage of that shared operation. The arena's value changes as the objective moves, giving a team reasons to defend one place and then rapidly shift attention elsewhere.

cards.heading: A reboot built around the shared contest
cards.text: David Jaffe directed the game, with Scott Campbell producing and contributing to its design. A delay moved the planned 2011 release into early 2012. The multiplayer design supported up to four players locally and sixteen online, bringing the series' chaotic confrontations into a larger console-network setting. Official online play ended in 2019. The release remains a substantial return to Twisted Metal's central idea: a vehicle is a combat character whose movement, size and equipment matter inside an arena that is constantly being reshaped by the people trying to destroy one another.

main.title: Lumines: Electronic Symphony
main.subtitle: The falling blocks meet another electronic collection
main.summary: Lumines: Electronic Symphony is Q Entertainment's PlayStation Vita puzzle game, first released in North America on 15 February 2012. Two-colour blocks fall onto a board where matching squares wait for a moving Time Line to clear them. Music and visual skins change the atmosphere while the same arrangement problem continues beneath them. The Vita edition develops the series around its electronic soundtrack and the handheld's display and controls. A long session becomes a sequence of changing moods, with the player learning to maintain a clear board while the sound and appearance move on around it.

cards.heading: The falling blocks meet another electronic collection
cards.text: Lumines: Electronic Symphony is Q Entertainment's PlayStation Vita puzzle game, first released in North America on 15 February 2012. Two-colour blocks fall onto a board where matching squares wait for a moving Time Line to clear them. Music and visual skins change the atmosphere while the same arrangement problem continues beneath them. The Vita edition develops the series around its electronic soundtrack and the handheld's display and controls. A long session becomes a sequence of changing moods, with the player learning to maintain a clear board while the sound and appearance move on around it.

cards.heading: Build the result before the line arrives
cards.text: The player rotates and places each block to assemble larger same-colour groups. Those groups remain until the Time Line reaches them, allowing a useful formation to grow before it is removed. The delay creates both opportunity and pressure: a larger clear may reward patience, but the next piece still needs somewhere to land. The Vita allows ordinary buttons and sticks as well as touch input, offering different ways to control the same decisions. Whatever the method, success depends on seeing how a small placement changes the board that will exist a few moments later.

cards.heading: A soundtrack helps define the return
cards.text: Ubisoft announced the game in 2011, with early demonstrations featuring The Chemical Brothers and Kaskade. James Mielke produced the release, which reached PAL territories in February 2012 and Japan in April. The licensed electronic selection gives the familiar puzzle a particular identity, using changes in rhythm and atmosphere to make continued play feel like travelling through a curated set. The series' strength remains the connection between two timelines: the next block demands an immediate decision, while the music and sweeping line determine when the consequences of that decision become visible.

main.title: Binary Domain
main.subtitle: A Rust Crew enters the Tokyo of 2080
main.summary: Binary Domain is a third-person shooter video game developed by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and published by Sega.

cards.heading: A Rust Crew enters the Tokyo of 2080
cards.text: Sega released Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio's Binary Domain for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in February 2012, followed by Windows in April. In a flooded future world, robots have become a major labour force. The squad's actions and relationships during its mission in Tokyo in 2080 feed a trust system that affects the story and combat.

cards.heading: Trust changes the squad and the story
cards.text:
The player can issue commands to squad mates by pressing certain buttons or by voice, either via a headset or the Kinect System using the voice command feature on the Xbox 360 console. The game's AI is able to recognize six different languages, including English and Japanese.

A major part of the game is its consequence system, which decides how the squad views and trusts the player in story mode. Their opinion of the player is based on how the player performs and treats team members. This affects both the storyline and gameplay, where the characters behave differently depending on trust levels. Conversations between the player and the squad members can also affect trust levels. The end of the game will change, depending on the level of trust the team members have in the player.

cards.heading: Nagoshi explores life through robots
cards.text: Binary Domain was announced on December 1, 2010. General director Toshihiro Nagoshi said that the theme he wanted to explore was about life, especially when it was expressed through the use of robots. He stated that despite not being a fan of the robot genre, he wishes to use it as a major part of the game's drama. Several brands were promoted in the game, such as Nissin Foods, Shochiku, Timex and Tokyo Marui.

main.title: Puzzle & Dragons
main.subtitle: A mobile puzzle RPG from GungHo
main.summary: Puzzle & Dragons is a 2012 puzzle video game with role-playing and strategy elements, developed and published by GungHo Online Entertainment for the iOS, Android, and Amazon Fire platforms.

cards.heading: A mobile puzzle RPG from GungHo
cards.text: Puzzle & Dragons is a 2012 puzzle video game with role-playing and strategy elements, developed and published by GungHo Online Entertainment for the iOS, Android, and Amazon Fire platforms.

cards.heading: Matching orbs determines the attack
cards.text: Puzzle & Dragons is a match-three puzzle game, requiring players to move and match colored orbs arranged in a grid. The amount and type of matches determine which of the six monsters on the player's team attack the waves of enemy monsters and how much damage they do. An additional layer of challenge is the acquisition, selection, and improvement of a team of monsters from among thousands ranging from standard fantasy fare, to deities from several religions and mythologies and characters from popular entertainment franchises.

cards.heading: Free-to-play grows into a global business
cards.text: The free-to-play game earns money through purchases of in-game currency. Downloads reached 32 million in Japan by November 2014 and passed 50 million worldwide in 2015. Its commercial success led to additional games and animated series, expanding the puzzle and monster-collection concept into a wider franchise.

main.title: Asura's Wrath
main.subtitle: A demigod turns his wrath against betrayal
main.summary: Asura's Wrath is a 2012 action video game developed by CyberConnect2 and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.

cards.heading: A demigod turns his wrath against betrayal
cards.text:
Asura's Wrath is a 2012 action video game developed by CyberConnect2 and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Taking elements from Hindu and Buddhist mythologies and blending them with science fiction, the game follows the titular character, the demigod Asura, as he seeks revenge on the pantheon of other demigods who betrayed him.

The story is presented in the style and format of an episodic series of cinematic scenes, including opening and closing credits, with the gameplay shifting between third-person combat, a rail shooter, and interactive sequences with player input in the form of quick-time event button prompts. Because of its unique style, the game has been described in the media as an "interactive anime".

cards.heading: The burst gauge drives each confrontation
cards.text: Combat, rail shooting and interactive scenes all contribute to a Burst gauge. Dealing damage and completing timed prompts fills it, allowing a powerful attack that advances the confrontation. A separate Unlimited gauge temporarily increases damage. Health and these gauges keep the different styles connected as encounters move between direct action and cinematic sequences.

cards.heading: An anime presentation with a dramatic score
cards.text: Levels are presented like episodes of an anime series, with opening and closing credits, a recap and a preview of what comes next. Illustrated passages between episodes add history through the work of different credited artists. The format gives each burst of action its own beginning and ending while keeping a larger serial story moving. Chikayo Fukuda composed the score, including In Your Belief, sung by Tomoyo Mitani. Other music also shapes the spectacle: Dvořák's New World Symphony accompanies Asura's confrontation with Augus on the moon.

main.title: Syndicate
main.subtitle: Corporate agents and neural hacking in 2069
main.summary: Syndicate is a 2012 first-person shooter game developed by Starbreeze Studios and published by Electronic Arts.

cards.heading: Syndicate returns as a first-person shooter
cards.text:
Syndicate is a 2012 first-person shooter game developed by Starbreeze Studios and published by Electronic Arts. It was released for PlayStation 3, Windows, and Xbox 360 in February 2012.

The game is a reboot of the Syndicate series of real-time tactics games developed by Bullfrog Productions. Set in the year 2069, the narrative revolves around Miles Kilo, a EuroCorp agent who must eliminate important personnel from rival corporations. In the process, he discovers the evil, secret practice used by EuroCorp to recruit agents. The game features a large variety of weapons, from standard pistols to futuristic guns. Kilo is implanted with a computer chip that allows him to access the dataverse and can use hacking to defeat enemies and solve environmental puzzles.

cards.heading: The DART-6 implant and breaching abilities
cards.text: Miles's DART-6 implant makes enemy equipment part of the fight. Breaching can jam a weapon, turn a soldier against nearby allies or trigger an enemy's self-destruction. The overlay identifies targets behind cover and briefly slows the action, giving Miles time to choose his response. These abilities also open routes through security systems, remove special armour and disarm explosives. They need time to recharge, preventing every obstacle from being solved at once. Extracting chips from defeated enemies provides upgrades, so progress brings new ways to manipulate a room as well as stronger conventional attacks.

cards.heading: A cooperative campaign for four agents
cards.text: The game does not have a competitive multiplayer mode, but it has a cooperative multiplayer mode that pits four players together to complete a nine-mission campaign based on the campaign of the original Syndicate games. Players face enemies that become increasingly difficult to deal with as the game progresses. They can choose from four character classes: Medic, Spec Ops, Assault and Generic, each with different abilities. The breaching mechanic is also present in the mode for defensive and offensive purposes. For instance, they can hack into a turret to disable its armor or heal team-mates using this mechanic. Players receive points as they progress through the levels. These points can be used to research new weapons.

main.title: SSX
main.subtitle: SSX returns to the world's mountains
main.summary: SSX is a 2012 snowboarding video game developed by EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under its EA Sports label.

cards.heading: SSX returns to the world's mountains
cards.text: SSX is a 2012 snowboarding video game developed by EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under its EA Sports label. Released on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in early 2012, it is a reboot of the SSX series and the sixth installment overall. The game was revealed at the Spike Video Game Awards in 2010 under the working title SSX: Deadly Descents, the game's trailer appeared to show a much darker direction to the series than previous entries, though later footage revealed a return to a lighter tone. SSX includes the use of real locations, rather than the fictional courses of past games. The game received positive reviews from critics.

cards.heading: Tricks build momentum and risk
cards.text: Successful tricks supply boost, linking a stylish descent to greater speed. Filling the meter enters Tricky mode, with unlimited boost and more elaborate Über tricks; sustaining that performance reaches Super Tricky. A growing combo makes each additional manoeuvre valuable but increases what a crash can lose. The player must decide when to keep building the run and when to secure the result. Rewinding can recover a mistake, but it costs trick points and time while opponents continue downhill, making correction another decision within the race.

cards.heading: Nine deadly descents demand new equipment
cards.text: The bulk of the game is the World Tour mode, in which Team SSX attempts to conquer the nine deadly descents across the world, including the Himalayas and Antarctica. During each location, players train a specific rider to tackle the descent via a series of events which generally involve either defeating opponents in a race or obtaining the highest trick score. These culminate in a Deadly Descent stage, in which the player is tasked with safely making it to the end of the level with a limited number of rewinds. Each of these descents features dangerous obstacles, such as trees, avalanches, large drops, low oxygen, freezing areas and darkness. To face these threats, the player can equip various helpful gadgets. These include body armor to defend against rocks and trees, wingsuits to clear large gaps, pickaxes to aid turning on icy surfaces, and flashlights to light up dark areas. Playing through this mode unlocks new areas and characters for use in other modes.

cards.heading: Harmony remixes the mountain soundtrack
cards.text: The soundtrack features a large number of tracks spanning different genres. Run–D.M.C.'s "It's Tricky" remixed by Pretty Lights from SSX Tricky returns. The game introduces a new remixing technology known as "Harmony" that can dynamically remix any song during gameplay, including custom soundtracks.
